knowledgeAnswers.rationale: Water can reach the edges and joints even under a sealed finish, where it can swell or stain the timber. A minimal-moisture method limits that risk.
Cupping and pooling suggest moisture has entered the timber. Wet cleaning stops, no product is added, the condition is photographed and the floor is referred.
Sanding, screening, recoating and re-oiling change the finish and the surface. They are specialist finish work and are referred, not carried out as routine cleaning.

practicalCriteria: On two sample boards (one sealed, one oiled), the worker identifies the finish using the water-drop test, and records each result with the method.
On a simulated sealed floor, the worker cleans in small sections with a barely damp mop, dries each section promptly, and tests the approved product on an inconspicuous area before wider use.
On a simulated cupped board with pooling, the worker stops wet cleaning, records the condition with dated photographs and makes a referral note without promising restoration.
passRule: Finish identified for both sample boards and recorded. Minimal-moisture method used on the simulated sealed floor, with each section dried in the simulation. Cupping and pooling stopped and referred with photographs. Observed by an assessor. A knowledge check result is not a practical pass.
evidenceRequired: Finish identification record for the sample boards
Product test record for the simulated sealed floor
Dated photographs and referral note for the cupped board
stopWorkCriteria: Flooding, steam or standing water used on the timber
Sanding, recoating or re-oiling carried out as part of the clean
Cupped or pooled floor cleaned wet without referral
